extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral/political philosophy (e.g., readers of Hume; philosophy students)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and judge the requirements and marks claimed for 'innate' (speculative and practical) principles in moral and epistemological debates; the text examines what would have to obtain for a principle to count as innate and objects to those claims with historical and conceptual examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal consent / universal assent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where then are those innate principles of justice, piety, gratitude, equity, chastity? Or where is that universal consent that assures us there are such inbred rules?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents implicitly require that innate principles be universally acknowledged by all societies (universal consent). The text rebuts this by citing widespread cultural differences (murders in duels considered honourable in some places, practices of exposing or killing children, ritual cannibalism, etc.) showing no universal moral rule across societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally allowed breach disproves innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: The generally allowed breach of it anywhere, I say, is a proof that it is not innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a purported innate practical rule is commonly and openly breached with public allowance in some society (e.g., exposing children, killing parents at a given age, rituals of abandonment), that fact counts as evidence against the rule being innate. Hume uses historical and anthropological examples to support this rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innate principles must produce certainty (knowledge of law/punishment)
rubrics_metrics.description: If anything be imprinted on the minds of all men as a law, all men must have a certain and unavoidable knowledge that certain and unavoidable punishment will attend the breach of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a practical principle to be truly innate as a duty, it must carry with it an immediate and unavoidable apprehension of a lawmaker and inevitable sanction (reward/punishment or a life after this). Hume argues such accompanying ideas (God, law, punishment, afterlife) are not themselves innate, so the supposed certainty cannot obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innateness requires constituent ideas to be innate
rubrics_metrics.description: Had those who would persuade us that there are innate principles not taken them together in gross, but considered separately the parts out of which those propositions are made, they would not, perhaps, have been so forward to believe they were innate. Since, if the IDEAS which made up those truths were not, it was impossible that the PROPOSITIONS made up of them should be innate...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposition cannot be innate unless the ideas composing it are innate; thus scrutiny must test whether the underlying simple ideas (identity, impossibility, duty, etc.) are present from birth. Hume argues they are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innate ideas should be present in children/newborns
rubrics_metrics.description: If we will attentively consider new-born children, we shall have little reason to think that they bring many ideas into the world with them... there is not the least appearance of any settled ideas at all in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One test for innateness is presence in infancy: genuine innate ideas/principles should be observable (clearly present and early) in young children. Hume contests this: newborns lack the supposed abstract ideas claimed as innate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innate principles must be propositional and intelligible (not mere commands or vague names)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Parents preserve and cherish your children.’ is so far from an innate truth, that it is no truth at all: it being a command, and not a proposition... To make it capable of being assented to as true, it must be reduced to some such proposition as this: 'It is the duty of parents to preserve their children.' But what duty is, cannot be understood without a law; nor a law be known or supposed without a lawmaker...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a moral rule to count as an innate truth it must be a clear propositional content (with intelligible constituent ideas). General words like 'virtue' or 'sins' are too vague to be innate unless their particulars are engraved as well. Hume stresses that many putative innate principles are expressed as commands or vague generalities which presuppose further concepts (law, reward, punishment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity/distinctness requirement for innate notions (avoid vague general words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor is the fourth proposition (viz. 'Men must repent of their sins') much more instructive, till what those actions are that are meant by sins be set down... it is impossible that God should engrave principles in words of uncertain meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine innate principles must be clear and determinate in content; they cannot plausibly be general labels (virtue, sin) without the specific actions these names cover being also innate. Hume argues that innate principles written in ambiguous terms would be useless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to corruption by education/custom (or else universality fails)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor will it be of much moment here to offer that very ready but not very material answer, viz. that the innate principles of morality may, by education, and custom, and the general opinion of those amongst whom we converse, be darkened, and at last quite worn out of the minds of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If innate principles can be 'blunted' or erased by education/custom, then they would not be universally evident; proponents must say whether innate principles are immune to such corruption (in which case they must appear in all people) or they are alterable (in which case they fail to provide the claimed universality). Hume exposes the incoherence of allowing both possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks/characters required to distinguish genuine innate principles
rubrics_metrics.description: I desire these men to say, whether they can or cannot, by education and custom, be blurred and blotted out; if they cannot, we must find them in all mankind alike, and they must be clear in everybody... When this is done, I shall be ready to embrace such welcome and useful propositions; and till then I may with modesty doubt; since I fear universal consent, which is the only one produced, will scarcely prove a sufficient mark to direct my choice, and assure me of any innate principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents must provide explicit 'marks and characters' that reliably distinguish genuine innate principles from adopted or culturally taught ones. Hume demands concrete criteria rather than mere appeals to alleged universal assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility/identity not plausibly innate unless simple ideas are present
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is impossible for the same thing to be, and not to be,' is certainly (if there be any such) an innate PRINCIPLE. But can any one think, or will any one say, that 'impossibility' and 'identity' are two innate IDEAS?...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even logical principles (identity, impossibility) would presuppose corresponding simple ideas; the test for innateness must show these elementary ideas are actually present. Hume argues our concepts of identity/impossibility are not evident in infancy and vary among people, undermining claims of their innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innate principles cannot be publicly renounced by whole societies
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to conceive that a whole nation of men should all publicly reject and renounce what every one of them certainly and infallibly knew to be a law; for so they must who have it naturally imprinted on their minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a whole society can publicly and professedly disown a rule without apparent contradiction or universal denunciation, that counts against the rule being innate. Hume uses historical examples of societies that practice and profess contrary norms to show this condition fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: If innate, principles need not be taught (should be immediately recognizable)
rubrics_metrics.description: But, in truth, were there any such innate principles there would be no need to teach them. Did men find such innate propositions stamped on their minds, they would easily be able to distinguish them from other truths that they afterwards learned and deduced from them...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine innate principle should be immediately apparent and recognisable without instruction; the absence of such easy identification in practice undermines claims of innateness. Hume points out that no catalogue of such principles exists because they are not self-evidently known.
